route that does not use Link R1. Accordingly, R1 Landowners respectfully show the following:

I. INTRODUCTION

On March 26, 2026, Oncor Electric Delivery Company (“Oncor”) and LCRA Transmission
Services Corporation (“LCRA TSC”) (collectively the “Applicants”) filed a joint application
(“Application”) with the Public Utility Commission of Texas to amend their certificates of
convenience and necessity for the proposed Bell County East Switch to Big Hill Substation 765-
kV Transmission Line Project (“Project”) in Bell, Burnet, Concho, Coryell, Lampasas, Llano,
Mason, McCullouch, Menard, Milam, Mills, San Saba, Schleicher, Tom Green, and Williamson
Counties.! In this Project, which has a length range of approximately 214 to 244 miles, the

Applicants propose the construction of a 765-kV transmission line consisting of steel lattice tower

1 Oncor & LCRA TSC Exhibit No. 1 (Joint Application)

 structures, which height ranges from 140 to 198 feet.” The estimated cost of the Project, excluding
station costs, ranges from $1,636,232,000 to $1,857,786,000. This is a long, expensive Project,
and given the overall involvement by pro se intervenors, attorneys, counties, and other interested
parties, this is also a highly contested, unwelcome Project that landowners want to avoid.

The Administrative Law Judges (“ALJs”) and the Public Utility Commissioners of Texas
(“Commission”) are tasked with determining which of the presented routes, including Requests
for Information (“RFI”) Routes, best satisfy the requirements of PURA § 37.056(c)(4)(A)-(D) of
the Texas Utilities Code and 16 TAC § 25.101 when looking at the data provided by Applicants
and Intervenors. This process is a balance of factors, not a math question, where all relevant
information should be considered.‘ In selecting a route, one choice is clear—the approved route
should not use Link R1.

R1 Landowners consists of seven Schleicher County property owners who are located in
the westernmost portion of the Study Area. This area of Schleicher County, along proposed Link
R1, is rural and consists of ranchland predominantly used for agriculture and hunting. There are
scattered homes located on these ranches and no industrial infrastructures are located along the
path, or in the immediate area.

Link R1 is a primary link in this Project and has the misfortune of being located on 85%
of the 1,246 routes identified by Applicants. Link R1 is also used on 78% of the 122 filed routes.*
Accordingly, Link R1 Landowners have been placed at a disadvantage due to so many routes using
Link R1.° The Applicants and other Intervenor experts focused their route selection attention on
the 122 filed routes, although PUC Staff Expert John Poole was able to review a few of the RFI
routes.’ With so few routes using link sequences that do not include Link R1, there was limited
attention, if not nonexistent, regarding alternative link sequences for routes in the western portion
of the Study Area. These alternative routes that do not use Link R1 are better matched and aligned

with the routing requirements for this Project as discussed in this Initial Brief.

N12 and Link P1—are already in an industrialized area consisting of and planning for wind
turbines and other industrial-related infrastructure. Link N12 and Link P1 parallel existing
transmission lines, impact zero habitable structures, and have a cheaper cost per mile than other

western link combinations.

II. ROUTING CRITERIA AND ROUTING IMPACTS

This Initial Brief does not address the Application, Route Adequacy, Notice, Public Input,
or Need. The focus of this Initial Brief is on Routing Criteria and why the ALJs should recommend,
and Commissioners should approve, a route that does not use Link R1 but instead uses Links N12
and P1.

A. Link N12 and Link P1 are the best links for routing through the western
25% of the Project.

Routes using link combination “N12-P1” are superior for routing through the western
portion of the Project® and are located in Concho, Tom Green, and Schleicher County. The
Applicants’ best meets route, Route 894, is 223.17 miles long and uses link sequence N3-P2-R1
as it traverses Menard and Schleicher County. This three-link sequence traverses approximately
54.29 miles, which is approximately 24.3% of the total length of Route 894.° The following link
sequences are used in various routes for this western portion of the Study Area, which account

for roughly 25% of the total length of the entire Project:

B. Link sequence “N3-P2-R1” costs more per mile than “N12-P1.”

When compared to routes that use link sequence “‘N3-P2-R1”, once a route crosses into
Menard County, the average cost per mile for routes using link sequence “N2-N11-N12” is cheaper
by $250.000. Link sequence “N3-P2-R1” totals approximately 54.29 miles at an average cost of
$6.016 million per mile. Alternatively, with routes that use link sequence “N2-N11-N12-P1”, is
slightly lower at 58.17 miles, with an average cost per mile reducing to $5.76 million per mile."

Similarly, when analyzing other routes that use link sequence “M5-N4-03-P2-R1”, such
as Staff Route 487, the overall length of this sequence totals approximately 54.86 miles with an
average cost of $5.84 million per mile. Whereas, when a route is diverted north using link
sequence “M6-N2-N11-N12-P1,” the overall length increases to 63.48 miles and the average cost
per mile is reduced by $143,273.00 per mile to approximately $5.7 million per mile.

A similar analysis can be done from the intersection of Links 03, P2, and O1. Beginning
at Link 03, if link sequence “P2-R1” is used at 33.259 miles, there is an average cost of $5.76
million per mile for these links. However, using link sequence “O1-P1”, which avoids Links P2
and R1 and avoids the habitable structures located on these links, the total mileage increases
slightly to 36.059 miles with a lower average cost of $5.71 million per mile.

The average cost per mile is cheaper when link sequences do not use link sequence “N3-
P2-R1. Although the use of the other link sequences marginally increases overall mileage, this
proves to be a reasonable trade-off that is offset by the decreased cost per mile and other
improvements discussed below. When taken into consideration with other factors, the slight length

increases when using any link sequence other than “N3-P2-R1” becomes more reasonable.

C. Positive transmission line paralleling increases when using “N2-N11-N12-
P1.”

Routing that increases the paralleling of compatible rights-of-way are positive routing
factors because the new route will reduce fragmentation of unencumbered land and can lessen
aesthetic impacts to the surrounding property. However, not all “paralleling” is equal. Calculating
the distance a route parallels apparent boundary lines is subject to interpretation by analyzing tax
parcels in each county, which is often out of date or requires additional research to determine a
landowner’s entire property. Although more accurate data for paralleling could be obtained
through reviewing additional tax parcels or with title work, it would be a very time-consuming
process.

A review of Intervenors’ direct testimonies can clarify and correct the data to determine
what properties are bisected. For example, the following Link N3 and Link R1 landowners all
testify their properties would be bisected: Angell Land and Livestock, LLC; JCS Ranch, L.L.C.;
JHET Ranch, LLC; Kaddo and Penni Kothmann; Menzies Residual Trust; MK3 Investments,
LLC; Rancho Bonito Livestock Company; Dennis Grafa; Gary and Katherine Johnson; 9-
Campbell Ranch, L.P.; Sharon Holman as Trustee of the Charles Ray Pfluger Shelter Trust; and
Chase B. Akin.'> For consistency, one would have to review direct testimony for every Intervenor
on every link to determine whether an actual property line—not an apparent boundary line—is
used.

as roads and transmission lines. The feedback to the Applicants from the Public Involvement

D. Community Values

The public’s engagement in the form of comments, protests, and intervenors should be
considered as part of community values.2? A review of the Applicants’ intervention map,
Applicants’ Exhibit 21, provides a visual of this engagement. Nearly all landowners along Link

Tom Green County on Link N12 and P1. This is especially true when you consider some
Intervenors are landowners along Link N3 and Link N12 (Angell Land and Livestock) and Link
RJ and Link P1 (Runge Ranch Company and Charles Ray Pfluger Shelter Trust).”!

E. Routes that use Link N12 and P1 would reduce aesthetic impacts by routing

proposed Link N3 purchased their property because of the aesthetics and landscapes
